characters.hamo: Hamo is the warm heart of Sêvan, a village of apple orchards under the mountains, and the voice of the whole road. He was born and grew up in Kobanî, where his father and mother still live with his younger brother and his two younger sisters; the road calls them only by who they are to him, never by name. As a young man he came to the village and stayed. He lives behind the blue gate with Hevalo, Bozo the donkey, Şêro the dog and the old apple orchard, and the village children call him Xalo Hamo. He speaks standard Kurmanji with the warmth and a few of the words of Kobanî. Steady, patient and easily pleased, he laughs at his own stories (often before the end of them), lifts the end of his full black moustache when he is pleased with you, and is prouder of that moustache than of anything he owns. A miss gets one raised eyebrow and a thoughtful look, never a cross word. He wears the traditional suit with a green piştên, keeps the orchard, drinks tea from dawn to dusk with far too much sugar, is never quite on time, and has a proverb or a tale for every moment. He says nearly every line of the road: he talks with you, and tells you about everyone else, while Xezo and Hevalo say their own few lines.
characters.xezo: Xezo is the young teacher at the village school. She comes from Amed and teaches the children of Sêvan their letters, and she lives in the village like any other neighbour. She is seen now and then, at the school with the children or at the market, and in her own scenes she speaks for herself, bright and kind: who she is, her lessons, her decision and her goodbye. The words of school and learning are hers wherever they come (dibistan, pirtûk, wane, tîp, the days of the school week), so a word card may show her even in another scene. Otherwise the road hears of her through what Hamo and the children say. Bright, quick and kind, she knows the city and the village alike. In the last chapters a school in Hewlêr, far away, offers her a post; she decides to go, says goodbye to the whole village, and leaves on the dawn bus from the blue gate.
characters.hevalo: Hevalo is a young male deer and the learner’s guide: he brings you to Hamo’s blue gate in the first lesson and walks the whole road beside you. His name means “O friend!” Curious about everything and quick on his feet, he hops when he is pleased, tilts his head when something puzzles him and pricks up his ears at anything new. He is always after apples and always the first suspect when apples go missing, cheeky in a sweet way and kind when you get something wrong. He talks a little, in a young voice: short, cheeky, warm lines (“Ez birçî me!”, “Sêva paşîn ji bo min e!”), never long sentences; anything longer Hamo tells for him, usually with a laugh. The words that are his he says wherever they come: sêv first of all, fruit, the orchard and its flowers, the animals, the weather and the sky, and his own ears, eyes, nose and belly. On the summer pastures he only has eyes for Zerê, a shy wild doe, and brings her every apple he can carry.

units.story: Hevalo, a young deer with a twitching nose and a weakness for apples, brings you up a lane of apple trees to a blue gate in Sêvan, a village of orchards under the mountains. Behind it lives Hamo: born in Kobanî, owner of the proudest black moustache in the valley and of more tea glasses than chairs. On your first day you say hello and thank you, take an apple (Hevalo takes three), drink your first tea, learn whose house this is and what everything is called, and when you don’t know a word you ask “Bi kurdî çi ye?” By night you can say what you want, discover that the apple basket is mysteriously empty, and wish everyone good night.

skills.grammar: “to be” as an ending: ez … im / me, tu … î / yî (Ez baş im. Tu çawa yî?); and Ez sêvê dixwim, I eat the apple, learnt whole
skills.grammarMd:
**Ez baş im.** I am well. In Kurmanji “am” and “are” are not words of their own: they are short endings after the word they go with.

- **ez … im** after a consonant, **ez … me** after a vowel: *Ez baş im.* · *Ez Hamo me.*
- **tu … î** after a consonant, **tu … yî** after a vowel: *Tu baş î?* · *Tu çawa yî?*
- *Sêv* → **Ez sêvê dixwim.** I’m eating the apple: the verb comes last, and *sêv*, a feminine noun, takes **-ê** as the thing you eat.

lessons.beat: Hevalo, the young deer who is your guide, trots you up a lane of apple trees to a blue gate. It swings open, and a man with a magnificent black moustache beams at you: “Silav!” He hands you a red apple. “Spas!” you say, and take a bite: “Ez sêvê dixwim.” Hevalo watches every bite, and the moment you look away, Hevalo sêvê dixwe: your apple.

new.en: I eat …, I’m eating … (tu … dixwî: you eat; … dixwe: he, she eats)

lessons.beat: “Ez Hamo me,” he says, and gives the end of his moustache a proud little lift. Another apple? “Erê, spas!” A third? Hamo teaches you the polite way out: “Na, spas.” Hevalo has never once said no to an apple. Then an apple drops from the tree onto Hamo’s head. “Ez baş im!” he announces, rubbing it, and he means it.

new.en: am (im after a consonant, me after a vowel)

lessons.beat: At the gate, your first whole conversation: Hamo says hello, asks how you are, and you ask him back. He is well, you are well, and Hevalo, with an apple in each cheek, is clearly very well. Then Hamo asks the deer how he is, and gets no answer at all, only crunching.

new.en: are (with tu: î after a consonant, yî after a vowel)
how (Tu çawa yî? How are you?)

lessons.beat: Hamo practises everything with you at the gate: hello, how are you, yes thanks, no thank you, I’m eating the apple. Then he tries his questions on Hevalo, who nods at any question with an apple in it and looks at the sky for the rest.

skills.grammar: ev … e / ye: this is … (Ev çay e.), and the question Ev çi ye?; Ez avê vedixwim, I drink the water, learnt whole
skills.grammarMd:
**Ev çay e.** This is tea. “Is” is an ending too: **e** after a consonant, **ye** after a vowel.

- *Ev nan e.* This is bread. · *Çay xweş e.* The tea is nice. · *Ev Hevalo ye.* This is Hevalo.
- To ask, put **çi** (what) where the answer would be: *Ev çi ye?* What is this? — *Ev sêv e.*
- *Av* → **Ez avê vedixwim.** I drink the water. *Çay* takes **-ê** too (*Ez çayê vedixwim*), but *nan* and *şîr* stay as they are (they are masculine): *Ez nan dixwim.* · *Ez şîr vedixwim.*

lessons.beat: Hamo sits you down under the oldest apple tree and comes back with a tray: a glass of tea, warm bread, water from the spring, and a bowl of milk for Hevalo, who is young enough to love it. You drink your tea, “Ez çayê vedixwim”, Hamo eats his bread, and Hevalo drinks his milk, loudly, and then pushes his nose into everything else in case it is an apple.

new.en: I drink …, I’m drinking … (tu … vedixwî: you drink; … vedixwe: he, she drinks)

lessons.beat: Hamo turns the tray into a game: he points, “Ev çi ye?”, and you answer. Tea, bread, water, apple. Then he points at the deer: “Ev çi ye?” — “Ev Hevalo ye!” Everything on the tray is xweş, says Hamo, and Hevalo agrees by eating the napkin.

new.en: is (e after a consonant, ye after a vowel)

lessons.beat: Halfway through his tea Hamo jumps up: he forgot the most important thing! Back to the blue gate he goes, opens it again with a bow and says it properly, “Bi xêr hatî!”, and teaches you the answer every guest gives, “Xêra Xwedê li we bê!”. Then “Fermo!”: a fresh glass of tea, very hot. Hamo blows on his glass, and Hevalo, helpfully, blows on the bread.

new.en: Welcome! (to one person; Bi xêr hatin! to more than one)
Thank you! (the answer to a welcome; word for word “may God’s good be on you”)
here you are; please, go ahead

lessons.beat: A second glass, a third, a fourth: Hamo pours, you name what is on the tray, and he gives his moustache a pleased little lift at every right answer. By the fifth glass Hevalo has eaten the bread, and the tray is mostly tea.

skills.grammar: navê min, navê te: my and your after the noun, joined by -ê (learnt as whole phrases); kî? who?
skills.grammarMd:
**Navê min Hamo ye.** My name is Hamo. *Min* is “me, my” and *te* is “you, your”; they come after the noun, which takes a small link, **-ê**: *navê min*, *navê te*.

- *Navê te çi ye?* What is your name? · *Ev kî ye?* Who is this? — *Ev Hevalo ye.*
- With *mal* the link is **-a**: *Ev mala min e.* This is my house. Chapter 2 shows why.

lessons.beat: Hamo realises he never asked your name. “Navê min Hamo ye. Navê te çi ye?” He writes your name in the dust with a stick so that he won’t forget it, and Hevalo rubs it out with a hoof. “Ev kî ye?” asks Hamo, pointing at the culprit, who looks at the sky.

Hamo shows you round: “Ev mala min e. Ew derî ye.” The blue gate creaks, the kitchen door sticks, and one small door he does not open. Hevalo stands in front of it, hungry as ever, because he knows exactly what is behind it: the apple store.

You point at everything and ask Hamo, “Bi kurdî çi ye?” He knows every word in the house, until you point at a strange old tool hanging over the stove and he has to admit it: “Ez nizanim!” Hevalo knocks the tray with his nose; “Bibore!” says Hamo for him, and the deer looks sorry for almost a second.

new.en: What is it in Kurdish? How do you say it in Kurdish?

lessons.beat: Hamo plays guess-who with you round the house and the photos on the wall: “Ev kî ye? Ev çi ye? Bi kurdî çi ye?” Hevalo pretends to be a chair to avoid the questions; Hamo sits on him, and the game ends in laughter.

skills.grammar: whole phrases first: Ez … dixwazim (I want …), … heye? / … tune (is there …? / there isn’t), and Were!, Bixwe!, Vexwe!
skills.grammarMd:
Some Kurdish is best learnt whole, before its grammar. Kurdish puts the verb last, so what you want comes first:

- **Ez nan dixwazim.** I want bread. · *Tu çi dixwazî?* What would you like? · *Hevalo sêvekê dixwaze.* Hevalo wants an apple.
- **Nan heye?** Is there bread? — *Erê, heye.* Yes, there is. · *Na, tune.* No, there isn’t. · **Were!** Come! · **Bixwe!** Eat! · **Vexwe!** Drink!

lessons.beat: Dinner. Hamo asks what you want, and now you can say it: “Ez nan dixwazim.” Hevalo wants one thing only and Hamo does not need to ask. “Sêv heye?” He looks in the basket: “Erê, heye. Bixwe!” For you it is “Bixwe, vexwe!”, which is Hamo’s whole idea of looking after a guest.

new.en: I want … (tu … dixwazî: you want; … dixwaze: he, she wants)
there is; is there …? (Çay heye? Is there any tea?)

lessons.beat: Hamo goes back to the basket for more apples. “Sêv tune!” The basket is empty, and a certain deer is lying very still under the table. “Hevalo, were!” Hevalo does not come. The water from the spring is cold, the tea is hot, and Hamo, who has a whole orchard, laughs it off with a “gelek spas” to the oldest apple tree.

Night falls on Sêvan. Hamo shows you to the guest room, “Şev baş!”, and in the morning he is at the gate with tea: “Roj baş!” You set off with Hevalo to see the village, “Bi xatirê te!”, and Hamo waves: “Bi xêr biçî!” Ten steps down the lane, Hevalo turns back for an apple.

new.en: Goodbye! (said by the one who leaves, to one person)
Go well! (the answer to “Bi xatirê te!”)

lessons.beat: Your first morning walk through the village with Hevalo: hello to everyone, yes, no, thank you, I want, I don’t know, goodbye; and back at the blue gate, Hamo with the tea, asking what you saw. Tomorrow, he says, the neighbours are coming.

units.story: The neighbours come to tea at Hamo’s: Nazê from next door with her son Baran, nine and full of questions, and her daughter Hêvî, six and shy until she isn’t, and then Dapîr Şemsê, the village grandmother, who leans on her stick and on everybody. On the guest-room wall hang photos of Hamo’s family, far away in Kobanî. Hêvî counts the hens with Dapîr and gets a different number every time; breakfast is spread on a cloth on the floor and Hamo puts five sugars in his tea; everyone says which animals they have, and Bozo the donkey puts his big grey head over the wall to make sure nobody forgets him. Hevalo has no apples, and makes sure everybody notices.

skills.grammar: the ezafe: -ê after a masculine noun, -a after a feminine one (bavê min, diya min); em, hûn, ew … in / ne
skills.grammarMd:
**Bavê min, diya min.** My father, my mother. A noun is joined to the word after it by a link: **-ê** for a masculine noun, **-a** for a feminine one: *bavê min*, *birayê min*, *navê wê* (her name); *diya min*, *xwişka min* (*dê* becomes *diya*; after a vowel a *y* slips in: *birayê*).

- With **em** (we), **hûn** (you, more than one) and **ew** (they), “are” is **in**, or **ne** after a vowel: *Em malbat in.* · *Hûn cîran in.*
- *Ew li Kobaniyê ne.* They are in Kobanî.

lessons.beat: Tea for the neighbours, and while it brews Hamo shows you the photo wall in the guest room. A man with a grand moustache: “Ev bavê min e.” A woman with laughing eyes: “Ev diya min e.” Both far away in Kobanî. Beside them hangs a photo of the neighbours’ children: “Navê wî Baran e. Navê wê Hêvî ye.”

new.en: her (of a woman: navê wê, her name)

lessons.beat: More photos: four children in a row in Kobanî, Hamo the tallest because he is standing on a stone. “Ev birayê min e. Ev xwişkên min in. Em malbatek in,” he says proudly, and straightens every frame, and then straightens them again.

new.en: are (with em, hûn, ew: in after a consonant, ne after a vowel)

lessons.beat: A knock at the blue gate: the neighbours have come, Nazê with a plate of warm bread, Baran, and Hêvî hiding behind her mother’s skirt, and with them Xezo, the young teacher from Amed. Hêvî starts a game, “Ez kî me?”, and everyone says what they are: Hamo is a man, Xezo is a woman, and Hevalo, very proudly, is an animal. Hamo explains who is who: they are neighbours, you are the guest, and Hevalo just lives in the orchard and eats it.

sayings.ku: Şêr şêr e, çi jin e, çi mêr e.
sayings.en: A lion is a lion, whether woman or man.

lessons.beat: Hamo shows the photos to the neighbours too, and everyone has a question: who is this, is she your mother, is he your brother? Then Baran finds the funniest photo of all, Hamo at ten with no moustache, and Hamo turns it to the wall, too late.

skills.grammar: numbers before the noun, which does not change (du sêv, sê mirîşk); çend? how many?; age with salî
skills.grammarMd:
**Sê sêv.** Three apples. A number comes before the noun, and the noun stays as it is: *yek sêv*, *du mirîşk*, *çar zarok*.

- **Çend?** How many? *Mirîşk çend in?* — *Sê mirîşk in.* Counting out loud, two and three are *didu* and *sisê*.
- **Tu çend salî yî?** How old are you? — *Ez şeş salî me.*
- As the object of a verb, or after **bi**, a counted noun still takes **-an**: *Hevalo pênc sêvan dixwe*, *bi pênc şekiran*.

lessons.beat: Nazê introduces her children properly: “Ev kurê min e, Baran. Ev keça min e, Hêvî.” Then Hêvî and Hamo count the hens in the yard. One, two… but the hens will not stand still, so the answer changes every time: yek, du, yek, du, du, yek. At the photo wall two is easy: “Ev du xwişkên min in.”

Dapîr Şemsê arrives, leaning on her stick and on Baran, and takes over the counting at once. “Çend mirîşk?” Three, she says. Four, says Hêvî. Hamo counts too and gets five, because he counted Hevalo. Dapîr is every child’s grandmother in Sêvan, and Baran explains that his own grandfather lives in the next village, with a donkey even older than Bozo.

Ages round the tea tray. Hêvî holds up her fingers: six. Hevalo, says Hamo, is five, or he eats like five deer, anyway. Hamo asks how many brothers and sisters you have; in his family there are four children: Hamo, his brother and his two sisters. Then he counts Dapîr’s children and runs out of fingers.

new.en: … years old (Ez şeş salî me. I am six.)

lessons.beat: Dapîr and Hêvî count the hens one last time and finally agree, just as one hen walks out of the gate. Everyone says how old they are and how many brothers and sisters they have, and Hamo counts his apples: there should be ten; there are nine. Hevalo looks at the sky.

skills.grammar: ne before the word for “not”: Ez ne birçî me; and the thanks of the table
skills.grammarMd:
**Ez ne tî me.** I am not thirsty. *Ne* goes before the word it says no to, and the ending stays: *Ez birçî me* → *Ez ne birçî me*. · *Ev ne çay e.* This isn’t tea.

- Do not mix it up with **ne** meaning “are” after a vowel: *Em çar xwişk û bira ne.* We are four brothers and sisters.

- **Noşî can be!** Enjoy! Said to someone who is eating or drinking.
- **Destê te sax be!** Thank you! To the one who cooked or served (word for word: may your hand be healthy).

lessons.beat: Next morning the neighbours are back for breakfast, spread on a cloth on the floor: cheese, eggs, bread, tea. Hamo boils eggs, seven for seven people, then counts the people again and boils one more for Hevalo, who does not eat eggs but likes to have his own.

Baran announces that he is nine, nearly ten, and therefore not a child any more; he drinks his milk to prove it and gets a white moustache, which Hamo inspects with great professional interest. Hevalo is offered yoghurt and says, with his whole face, that it is not an apple.

new.en: not (with the copula: ez ne … im)

lessons.beat: Nazê made the bread, and Hamo teaches you what to say to her: “Destê te sax be!” Whenever anyone drinks he says “Noşî can be!” You are thirsty, so he keeps filling your glass, and every time you say thank you, he fills it again.

new.en: Thank you! (for food or help; word for word: may your hand be healthy)

lessons.beat: The breakfast cloth is spread in the yard for everyone. Hamo hands round bread, cheese, eggs and yoghurt, you thank Nazê properly for everything, and Hamo says “Noşî can be!” to every single mouthful, Hevalo’s included.

skills.grammar: having: the thing, then its owner, then heye / hene / tune (Kerekî min heye.); -ek for “a”
skills.grammarMd:
**Kerekî min heye.** I have a donkey (word for word: a donkey of mine is). The thing comes first, then its owner, then **heye**; **-ek** means “a”, and grows to **-ekî** (masculine) or **-eke** (feminine) before *min*.

- **hene** for more than one: *Du xwişkên min hene.* I have two sisters.
- **tune** for none: *Pisîkeke min tune.* I don’t have a cat.

lessons.beat: Everyone says which animals they have. Nazê has a cat; Dapîr has hens, a goat and opinions about everything; Hamo has a dog, Şêro, who guards the orchard and sleeps through it, and a donkey, Bozo, who chooses that moment to put his big grey head over the wall. Bozo is big, says Hamo, in body and in stubbornness. Hamo counts his family the same way: “Du xwişkên min hene. Birayekî min heye.”

Hêvî is little, says Baran; Hêvî says she is not. Baran says his friends at school are all big; Hêvî says her friend is Hevalo, whose very name means “friend!”, and that settles it. Meanwhile Hamo puts one sugar in his tea, then another, and another (five, Hêvî counts) and calls it a little sweetness.

Dinner with everyone at Hamo’s. “Kerem bike!” he says, passing round the bread, and when Hêvî counts all the way to ten without a mistake he calls out “Aferîn!”. Hamo asks where you are from, and tells you his own answer: from Kobanî, and from Sêvan. Meanwhile Hevalo eats the bread you were holding.

new.en: Where are you from? (Ez ji … me: I’m from …)

lessons.beat: A game at dinner: everyone says one thing they have and one they don’t. Hamo has a donkey, a dog and an orchard; he has no cat. Hevalo has no apples, so everyone gives him one, and now he has six, and Hamo has none.

units.story: Hamo shows you his house, all the way up to the flat roof where everyone sleeps on summer nights, and the clay tenûr in the yard where Dapîr bakes bread. You learn the colours of the village (the blue gate, the red apples, the green leaves, Dapîr’s white goat) and where things are: on, under, in, in front of and behind, while Hevalo hides apples in every one of those places. A game of “touch your nose” goes wrong when Hevalo joins in, and an apple shared under the walnut tree by the spring loses its other half to a certain deer. Then Hamo walks you through the village: the school, where Xezo, the young teacher from Amed, teaches the children their letters, the shop, the spring and the hills. Tomorrow is market day in the town.

skills.grammar: this and that after li: li vê odeyê (feminine, -ê), li vî …-î (masculine); li vir, li wir
skills.grammarMd:
**Li vê odeyê.** In this room. **Li** means in or at, and **ji** from. After them and the other little words of place, *ev* becomes **vê** with a feminine noun, which takes **-ê**, and **vî** with a masculine noun, which takes **-î**: *li vê malê*, *ji vî deriyî*.

- *Ew* becomes **wê** and **wî** in the same way: *li wê odeyê* in that room.
- With more than one: **van** and **wan**, and the noun takes **-an**. · *li vir* here, *li wir* there.

lessons.beat: Hamo gives you the house tour with enormous ceremony, as if you were a visiting governor: “Ev ode ye. Ev pencere ye. Ev mase ye.” Hevalo follows and inspects every chair, in case an apple is sitting on it. One is.

In every room something is in the wrong place: a hen on the bedding, a shoe on the table, Bozo’s nose through the window from the yard. Hamo points it all out, in this room, in that room, here, there, and carries the hen back to the yard, where she gives him a very offended look.

new.en: this, these (after a preposition: li vê malê)
that, those (after a preposition: li wê malê)

lessons.beat: Up the ladder to the flat roof, where everyone sleeps on summer nights under the stars; down in the yard, the round clay tenûr where Dapîr bakes bread. “Rûne!” says Hamo, and you sit on the roof with tea and warm tenûr bread. On the table lies a map of Sêvan, and Hevalo sniffs it all over, in case an apple is drawn on it.

Hamo gives you the house tour once more, faster, and you name everything as you go: this room, that window, the beds, the roof, the yard and the tenûr. Then he finds his own house on the map of Sêvan, and Hevalo checks every chair again, in case another apple has turned up.

skills.grammar: adjectives after the noun, joined with the same link: sêva sor, deriyê şîn, mala spî
skills.grammarMd:
**Sêva sor.** The red apple. An adjective comes after its noun, joined with the same link as *navê min*: **-a** for a feminine noun, **-ê** for a masculine one: *sêva sor*, *mala spî*; *nanê germ*, *deriyê şîn* (after a vowel the link is **-ya** / **-yê**).

- *Sêv sor e.* The apple is red: with *e* at the end, it says what the apple is like.
- *Rengê sêvê çi ye?* What colour is the apple?

lessons.beat: You start in Hamo’s own orchard: red apples on every tree, and the blue gate. Hamo declares red the best colour in the world, because of the apples, and blue the second best, because of the gate. Hevalo votes for red by eating one.

A walk through the lanes of Sêvan, which has a hundred yellow flowers and a hundred old doors. Hamo shows you the new door he made last year, which already looks older than the old ones. Hevalo eats three yellow flowers, to see whether yellow tastes like apples.

“Binêre!” Hamo points: Dapîr’s white goat with her long white beard, and Hamo’s own black moustache, the two finest in the village, he says, and the goat does not disagree. Then she starts on Dapîr’s flowers, and Hamo saves them with a piece of bread.

You name the colours of Sêvan with Hamo: the blue gate, the red apples, the green leaves, the white goat and the black dog. But who put fresh yellow paint on the window this morning? Hêvî giggles behind her hands, with yellow on her fingers.

skills.grammar: where things are: li ser, li bin, li ber, li pişt, di … de, with -ê on a feminine noun (li ser masê); Li ku ye?
skills.grammarMd:
**Sêv li ser maseyê ye.** The apple is on the table. The words of place come before the noun, and a feminine noun after them takes **-ê**: *li ser maseyê*, *li bin dara gûzê* under the walnut tree.

- **li ser** on · **li bin** under · **li ber** in front of · **li pişt** behind · **di … de** in: *Nan di tenûrê de ye.*
- **Li ku ye?** Where is it? — *Li vir e.* It’s here.

lessons.beat: Hamo cannot find his cap anywhere, not on the table, not under the bed, until Hêvî points: it is on his head, and has been all morning. “Ser!” she says, patting her own head, and the game of the day begins.

Hêvî’s game: Hamo calls out a part of the body and everyone touches it. Eyes! Ears! Head! Hevalo touches everything with his nose, mostly other people’s ears. Then lunch, “Destên xwe bişo!”, and the bread comes out of the tenûr, hot, right in front of everyone.

Under the walnut tree by the spring Hamo shares an apple with you: half for you, the other half for him. But where is the other half? Behind the tree there is a nose, and the other half is in Hevalo’s mouth. Never mind, says Hamo: Grandma Şemsê has plenty of apples.

Lunch is ready, but where is everyone? Şêro is under the table, the cat is out in the yard, and Hevalo’s nose is behind the walnut tree again. You find them all with Hamo, wash your hands and sit down to eat.

skills.grammar: plurals: no ending on its own (du mal), -ên before another word (malên spî), -an after a word of place (li gundan)
skills.grammarMd:
**Malên spî.** White houses. A plural noun on its own has no ending (*du mal*, *gelek dar*); before another word it takes **-ên**, and after a word of place **-an**.

- *zarokên gund* the village children · *sêvên sor* red apples
- *li gundan* in villages · *ji zarokan re* for the children
- A few words change their last vowel after a word of place: *bajar* → *li bajêr* in town, *çiya* → *li çiyê* on the mountain.

lessons.beat: Hamo walks you through the village. Here is the school: through the open window you hear the children reading aloud with their teacher, Xezo, the young teacher from Amed. Here is the shop, which sells everything and is never open when you need it. And here is the spring, where the water is so cold that Hevalo drinks it with his eyes shut.

From the flat roof you can see it all: the mountain above the village, the road down to the town where the market is, a flock of sheep on the hill and Ferhad’s cow in the field. The sun goes down behind the mountain, and Hamo says it does that every evening just to show off.

In the evening the birds sing in the apple trees and the children run in the lanes. Hamo has news: today is for resting, but tomorrow is market day in the town! Now, he says, tea. Hevalo cannot keep still: he has heard there are apples in the town that he has not eaten yet.

From the roof at sunset you name the whole village with Hamo: the school, the shop, the spring, the mountain, the sheep, and the town far below. Tomorrow you will all go down: Hamo, you, Hevalo, and Bozo, if Bozo agrees.

units.story: Market day in the town below the village. Hamo, Hevalo and you go down the road with Bozo, who carries the empty baskets and stops at every flower. Now the verbs come alive in the present tense: going, coming, seeing, saying, knowing, wanting, eating. At the market Hamo knows every seller, and Mîrza the fruit seller best of all: they haggle like the old friends they are, and Mîrza always wins. Hamo buys what is on his list and several things that are not, takes far too much sugar in Mîrza’s tea, and gets his numbers in a muddle once the prices pass a hundred. Then an apple basket is found empty, everyone says “Ez nizanim”, and a certain deer has a very round belly. By sunset, with Bozo groaning under the bags on the road home, you can say what you want and what you don’t, and what it all costs.

skills.grammar: the present tense: di- + the present stem + -im, -î, -e, -in; çûn (diç-), dîtin (dibîn-), gotin (dibêj-), kirin (dik-), and hatin (tê-)
skills.grammarMd:
**Ez diçim bazarê.** I am going to the market. The present is **di-** + the verb’s present stem + an ending: **-im** (I), **-î** (you), **-e** (he, she, it), **-in** (we, you, they).

- *çûn* to go: *diçim, diçî, diçe, diçin* · *dîtin* to see: *dibînim* · *gotin* to say: *dibêjim* · *kirin* to do: *dikim*
- *hatin* to come has no di-: *ez têm, tu têyî, ew tê, em tên*.

lessons.beat: Market day. Bozo carries the empty baskets down the road, Hamo walks in front and Hevalo is everywhere at once. “Em diçin bazarê! Tu jî têyî?” Of course you are coming. Bozo stops at every pretty flower and Hamo says he is admiring the view; Hamo stops at every neighbour and says the same.

On the way Hamo names everything he sees and has something to say about all of it: the river, the mountain, a hen who has followed you all the way from the village. At the river he stops to look at his moustache in the water and makes it even more magnificent. “Tu çi dikî?” you ask. “Ez li simbêlê xwe dinêrim,” he says, as if it were obvious.

new.en: to look (li … nêrîn: to look at)

lessons.beat: The market roars with voices. Hamo knows every seller and what each one sells, and he knows Mîrza best of all: his old friend, who sells the best fruit in the valley and talks even more than Hamo. Mîrza wants to know whether you speak Kurdish. You do! Hevalo stands very still beside the apples. Only looking, says Hamo. For now.

Hamo takes you round the whole market and tells you what everyone is doing: Mîrza is selling, the baker is shouting, a boy is going home with a goat, and Bozo is eating the flower seller’s flowers. You tell him what you can see, and he says you see more than he does.

skills.grammar: more presents: dixwazim (xwestin), dixwim (xwarin), vedixwim (vexwarin), dikarim (karîn)
skills.grammarMd:
**Tu çi dixwazî?** What would you like? Some verbs have a present stem quite unlike their name, so learn the two together:

- *xwestin* to want: **dixwazim** · *xwarin* to eat: **dixwim, dixwî, dixwe** · *vexwarin* to drink: **vedixwim** (the *ve-* stays in front of *di-*)
- *karîn* can: **dikarim**: *Ez dikarim!* I can! · *Tu dikarî?* Can you?

lessons.beat: Hamo reads his list aloud at the vegetable stall: tomatoes, potatoes, “ji kerema xwe”, and then whatever else catches his eye, which is everything. The seller asks what he wants to eat this week. Fruit, says Hamo, and looks at the apples; Hevalo looks at them too.

Hamo says he can carry everything, can find the best honey in the market, and can tell a fresh fish from an old one by its eyes. He carries two kilos and gives the rest to Bozo; he finds the honey by following the bees; the fish looks back at him, and he decides on meat.

Mîrza makes tea for his old friend. “Hinek şekir?” Hamo takes one spoonful, then a second, then a third, then a fourth, and Mîrza cries “Zêde!”: too much! Hamo says the sugar is for his voice, which he needs for haggling. Then he asks you how you take yours, and pours it himself, with sugar.

Lunch on a bench: bread, cheese, a little honey and tea. Everyone is eating, except Hevalo, who is suddenly not hungry at all and gazing at the mountain. Hamo asks what everyone wants for dinner; Hevalo still doesn’t want anything, which has never happened before.

skills.grammar: numbers to a thousand (bîst û yek, sî, çil, pêncî, sed, hezar) and prices with bi: Bi çend e? Bi pêncî ye.
skills.grammarMd:
**Bi çend e?** How much is it? — **Bi pêncî ye.** It’s fifty. Tens and ones are joined with **û**: *bîst û yek* 21, *sî û pênc* 35, *sed û deh* 110.

- *bîst* 20 · *sî* 30 · *çil* 40 · *pêncî* 50 · *sed* 100 · *hezar* 1000
- *du sed* 200, *sê hezar* 3000: the number before *sed* or *hezar* says how many.

lessons.beat: Hamo reads the prices on the stalls aloud and is shocked by every one of them. Twenty for grapes! Thirty for a basket! “Hemû bi çend e?” he asks one seller, pointing at the whole stall, just to see the man’s face. He counts his money three times; it does not get any more.

Haggling with Mîrza over a basket of apples: “Bi pêncî ye.” — “Pêncî? Biha ye! Çil!” — “Çil? Na!” Up and down they go for ten minutes, while the onion seller next door sells three kilos to people who just pay. In the end Hamo pays fifty and says it was cheap. “Bes e!” says Mîrza, and they both laugh.

Hamo reads out the prices: grapes twenty, onions fifty, apples forty, a hundred and ten in all, and a thousand for a carpet, which he finds very expensive. Then you both want to pay, and Hamo wins, because you are his guest. He gives Mîrza a little extra for the tea, and the sugar.

Hamo adds it all up once more: the potatoes, the fish, the honey, the basket of apples, Mîrza’s tea. He has twenty left, exactly the price of a glass of tea, and he spends it on tea, because Mîrza’s tea is good, and cheap.

skills.grammar: the negative present: na- in place of di- (naçim, naxwazim, nayêm), and ni- with zanîn and karîn (nizanim, nikarim)
skills.grammarMd:
**Ez naxwazim.** I don’t want it. In the present, **na-** takes the place of *di-*: *diçim* → **naçim**, *dixwim* → **naxwim**, *têm* → **nayêm**.

- *zanîn* and *karîn* take **ni-**: **nizanim** I don’t know, **nikarim** I can’t.
- **Kes nizane!** Nobody knows! *Hîç* makes it stronger: *Ez hîç nizanim.* I have no idea at all.

lessons.beat: An apple basket at the market is empty. Who ate the apples? Nobody knows. Bozo looks away. Hevalo shakes his head very, very fast: “Ez nizanim! Ez hîç nizanim!” “Çima?” asks Mîrza. Nobody knows that either.

new.en: not (with zanîn and karîn: nizanim, nikarim)
person; anyone (with a negative verb: nobody)

lessons.beat: The basket is empty, but somebody’s belly is very full. Hamo goes round looking for the apples, with you as his assistant. Is it true that Hevalo was by the basket? Hevalo says that is wrong, but there is apple peel on his nose.

new.en: to walk around; li … gerîn: to look for

lessons.beat: Hamo swears that Hevalo never eats apples and does not even like them, but Hevalo has apple all over his face. Nobody believes Hamo, not Mîrza and not the neighbours; then even Hamo laughs and pays for the apples. Then his phone rings: it is Nazê, the neighbour, asking how the market is.

new.en: to like, to love (ji … hez kirin)

lessons.beat: Home at sunset, Bozo groaning under the bags. On the road you and Hamo go over the day: what you saw, what you bought, what it cost and who ate the apples. Hevalo looks at the sky, and at the blue gate he is the first one in.

units.story: A week in Sêvan, by the calendar and the clock. Dapîr’s calendar by the stove fills up with days; the months and birthdays are counted (Hamo does not know his own birthday; his mother does, but she is in Kobanî). Hamo’s day runs on tea: up with the rooster, tea, the orchard, tea, a nap of “five minutes”, tea, and he is late for everything, cheerfully. Baran explains the school week (his teacher says reading comes before football, always). Hamo gives his solemn word to be on time for the Saturday bus to town, and on Saturday everyone reaches the square just in time to see it disappear round the bend; the next one is in the evening, and there is always time for tea.

skills.grammar: the days of the week, from Şemî (Saturday); roja Şemiyê (on Saturday); îro, sibe, duh, dusibe
skills.grammarMd:
**Îro Şemî ye.** Today is Saturday. The Kurdish week starts on Saturday: *Şemî* Saturday, *Yekşem* Sunday, *Duşem* Monday, and on to *Pêncşem* Thursday.

- “On Saturday” is **roja Şemiyê**: *roj* with its link, then the day with -ê: *roja Yekşemê*, *roja Duşemê*.
- *duh* yesterday · *îro* today · *sibe* tomorrow · *dusibe* the day after tomorrow

lessons.beat: Dapîr’s calendar hangs by the stove. Hamo explains the week to you, starting, as every Kurdish week does, on Saturday, and this Saturday there is a day out in Kobanî. “Kengî em diçin?” asks Hêvî, every five minutes. Saturday, says Hamo. And Sunday? Sunday is a holiday, he says; so is every day, if you ask him.

Baran explains his school week: on Monday he reads, on Tuesday he reads more, and his teacher says reading comes before football and after breakfast, always. Hamo nods wisely and says that in his day they read under the walnut tree, which is why he can only read in the shade.

Hamo plans the rest of the week out loud: on Wednesday he bakes bread with Dapîr; on Thursday he writes to his mother in Kobanî, which takes all day because he keeps crossing out the jokes. Then he asks you how long you will stay in Sêvan: a week or two, you say. And Hevalo? As long as there are apples, says Hamo.

Everyone writes their plans on Dapîr’s calendar: Baran writes “school” on every day but one; Hamo writes “çay” on every day and “Kobanî!” on Saturday; Hevalo, with a little help, gets “sêv” on every day. Then Dapîr circles Saturday in red, twice.

skills.grammar: months and ordinals: Adar, Nîsan, Gulan, Hezîran; yekem, duyem; di Adarê de (in March); … pîroz be!
skills.grammarMd:
**Newroz di Adarê de ye.** Newroz is in March. A month after *di … de* takes **-ê**: *di Nîsanê de* in April, *di Gulanê de* in May.

- **yekem** first, **duyem** second: *roja yekem* the first day · *meha duyem* the second month
- **Rojbûna te pîroz be!** Happy birthday!

lessons.beat: Hamo names the months as if they were old friends: Adar brings Newroz, Nîsan brings the blossom on the apple trees. Every month has a job, he says, and every year is better than the one before, except this year, which has been the best so far. And Friday? Friday is for tea and doing nothing, every week of the year.

Baran asks everyone’s birthday. His is in Gulan; Hêvî’s is in Hezîran, and she reminds everyone every day about the present. Hamo does not know his own birthday: his mother knows, but she is in Kobanî. Dapîr says it was the day of the big snow. Hamo says that was the first snow of the year; Dapîr says the second.

It is your birthday, and Hamo is the first to say “Rojbûna te pîroz be!” His own birthday? “Bîra min nayê,” he admits: his mother knows, and she is in Kobanî. And your present? “Xem neke!” he says: he remembers. Meanwhile Hevalo is hungry again, and Dapîr gives you an extra spoonful of honey.

new.en: Congratulations! (Rojbûna te pîroz be! Happy birthday!)
memory (bîra min tê: I remember; bîra min nayê: I don’t remember)

lessons.beat: Hamo and the children count the days to Saturday and the months to Newroz, and say whose birthday falls in which month. Baran wants to know why there is no month for apples; Hevalo agrees.

skills.grammar: telling the time: Demjimêr çend e? Demjimêr sê ye. sê û nîv, heft û deh xulek; at a time: di demjimêr heftan de
skills.grammarMd:
**Demjimêr çend e?** What time is it? — **Demjimêr sê ye.** It’s three o’clock. *Nîv* is half, and minutes past the hour follow **û**: *sê û nîv* half past three, *heft û deh xulek* ten past seven.

- “At” a time is **di demjimêr … de**, with the number in **-an**: *di demjimêr heftan de* at seven, *di demjimêr diduyan de* at two; *yek* takes **-ê**: *di demjimêr yekê de* at one.
- *sibeh* morning · *nîvro* noon · *êvar* evening · *şev* night

lessons.beat: Hamo owns three clocks, and each of them says a different time: one says eleven, one says twelve, one a quarter past something. He trusts the one that says it is time for tea. In the morning it is always time for tea, he explains, and in the evening too.

Hamo describes his day with pride: he wakes with the rooster, very early, gets up when the tea is ready, washes at the spring and, after lunch, goes to sleep for “just five minutes”. The five minutes last an hour. Sleep is good, he says; after tea, it is the best thing there is.

new.en: to sleep, to go to bed

lessons.beat: You time Hamo’s morning. “Five minutes” is an hour; “I’m coming” is two. Lunch is at noon, and Hamo arrives at one, delighted. Nazê laughs over the wall: it has been like this for twenty years. Hamo says he is never late; everyone else is just early.
Hamo’s whole day, hour by hour, from tea at seven to tea at nine at night, with a short nap in the middle that is not short, and lunch, which is at noon for everyone else.

skills.grammar: how often: her roj, her gav, carinan, gelek caran; the present for what you do again and again
skills.grammarMd:
**Ez her roj çay vedixwim.** I drink tea every day. The present also says what you do again and again:

- **her roj** every day · **her gav** always · **carinan** sometimes · *gelek caran* often (*car* is a time, an occasion)
- *Ez carinan dereng im.* I am sometimes late. — *Her gav!* says Nazê.

lessons.beat: Hamo admits that he is sometimes late. Nazê coughs. Hamo admits that he is often late. Dapîr coughs. Hamo admits nothing more, and goes to the orchard to work, which mostly means telling the apple trees what work he has to do today.

new.en: time, occasion (cara yekem: the first time)

lessons.beat: Baran explains how the bus works: it leaves the square for the town at eight every day and waits for nobody, only for the driver’s brother. Hêvî wants to play on the bus; Baran wants to learn to drive it. “Belê, belê,” says Hamo to everything, already planning a glass of tea at five to eight.

The bus to town leaves the square at eight sharp on Saturday, with no time for tea. Hamo gives his solemn word: “Soza min soz e!” If the bus will not stop for him, he says, he will run after it, with Hevalo. Get up early, you tell him; he is ready, he says.

Saturday morning, and you wake Hamo at half past eight: the bus leaves at eight. Everyone runs to the square; Hevalo races after the bus, but it is gone round the bend. The next one is in the evening, and Hamo knows what to do in between: drink tea.

units.story: A town, and being a guest and a host. A minibus takes you to Kobanî, where Hamo grew up: the town has grown since he was a boy and he gets lost in it, but there are the crowded market, the bakery where he bought bread as a boy of seven, the old bookshop, and Miştenûr hill above the roofs. At the table the orders never stop (“Werin hundir! Rûnin! Bixwe! Vexwe! Neke! Neçe!”), his sister’s children call their uncle Xalo and climb all over him, and an old photo shows who is who: this is my father, this is my mother, these are my brother and my two sisters. Then snow is forecast, and you must go back early, before the road closes. Orders fill the house, and so do divê and dikarim.

skills.grammar: finding the way: li rastê, li çepê, rasterast; bajar becomes bajêr after a word of place (li bajêr)
skills.grammarMd:
**Li rastê, li çepê, rasterast.** On the right, on the left, straight on. *Kolan li rastê ye.* The street is on the right.

- After *li*, *ji* or *bi*, *bajar* becomes **bajêr**: **li bajêr** in town, **ji bajêr** from town. With a word after it, it stays *bajar*: *li bajarê min* in my town.
- *Mal dûr e?* Is the house far? — *Na, nêzîk e.* No, it’s near.

lessons.beat: Ferhad’s tractor rattles everyone down to the main road, Hevalo in the trailer among the apple boxes. There a minibus driver squeezes you all in and sells Hamo tickets for everyone, Hevalo included. Kobanî is far; the driver is fast. “Hêdî, hêdî!” says Hamo, holding his moustache with both hands.

Kobanî has grown since Hamo was a boy, and every new street looks like the last one. He reads the signs aloud and turns left every time a sign says right, and for the first time in his life he is lost in his own town. “Here rasterast!” he tells himself. It works, eventually.

Kobanî at last: the crowded market, new shops where the old ones were, and Miştenûr hill high above the roofs. You ask Hamo about everything you see, while Hevalo climbs onto a flat roof for a better view, until Hamo calls him down.

The house where Hamo grew up, his father’s house at the corner, with the old fig tree still in the yard. Hamo shows you everything from the gate: the window he climbed out of, the step he fell down, the street where he got lost today.

skills.grammar: the imperative: bi- + present stem + -e for one, -in for more (bide, bidin); were, here, rûne without bi-; “don’t” with ne- (neke, neçe)
skills.grammarMd:
**Werin, rûnin!** Come in, sit down! An order to one person ends in **-e**, to more than one in **-in**, and most take **bi-** in front: *bide / bidin* give, *bibêje / bibêjin* say, and *bixwe* eat.

- Some have no bi-: *were* come, *here* go, *rûne* sit, *derkeve* go out, *vexwe* drink.
- “Don’t!” is **ne-** in place of bi-: *neke!* don’t, *neçe!* don’t go, *netirse!* don’t be afraid.

lessons.beat: “Werin hundir! Rûnin!” Hamo welcomes you in, and his sister’s children pour out of the house: Hamo is their uncle, their mother’s brother, so he is Xalo to all four of them, and all four climb on him at once.

new.en: to go out, to come out
uncle (your mother’s brother); xalo is also how you call an older man warmly

lessons.beat: At the table the orders never stop: “Bixwe! Vexwe! Bide min! Bibêje!” Nobody may stand up from it. Hamo’s uncle and aunt come round from next door with more food, and every guest hears the same: “Mala me mala we ye.” Hamo eats everything he is given and is given everything again.

You are Hamo’s guest, and a little afraid of Şêro, his dog: “Netirse!” says Hamo, Şêro will not hurt you. You want four sugars in your tea: “Neke!” You want to go to the market after tea: “Neçe!”, dinner is ready. And when you say you are full: “Bixwe!”

After dinner Hamo brings out an old photo, forty years old: his father and mother, and four children in a row. He shows you who is who: this is my father, this is my mother, this is me, this is my brother, and these are my two sisters. You may hold it, gently.

skills.grammar: divê, dikarim and dixwazim with the bi- form (divê ez biçim, ez dikarim bêm); bila ew bixwe (let him eat)
skills.grammarMd:
**Divê ez biçim.** I must go. After *divê* (must), *dikarim* (I can) and *dixwazim* (I want), the next verb takes **bi-** instead of *di-*: *Ez dikarim bibînim.* · *Ez dixwazim bixwim.*

- *hatin* has its own form: **bêm, bêyî, bê, bên**: *Ez dikarim bêm.* I can come.
- **bila** + the same form: *Bila ew bixwe!* Let him eat!

lessons.beat: Hamo makes a list of everything he must do in Kobanî: climb Miştenûr, buy a book for his father, eat the town’s bread, and visit his aunt, his mother’s sister, who will be cross if he doesn’t. Then he reads it aloud and adds “drink tea” to every line, because that is necessary too.

new.en: the form after divê, dikarim and dixwazim (biçim: go)
let (bila ew bê: let him come)

lessons.beat: Who washes the dishes? In Hamo’s house, he says, women and men both help, and every man in the room suddenly has to rest. You ask whether you may go up Miştenûr instead: maybe, says Hamo, after you help.

Up the hill to the old bookshop where Hamo bought his first books of stories. The bookseller is just closing, but he opens the door again for five minutes, and Hamo asks for a book of proverbs for his father, who knows so many proverbs that he is a book himself.

new.en: to take, to hold; to close

lessons.beat: Hamo gives his father the book of proverbs, and his father laughs: he knows half of them already. He reads them aloud, correcting the book as he goes, and everyone must say each one after him. It is late, says Hamo’s mother; one more, says his father, and reads ten.

skills.grammar: getting about with bi + -ê (bi trênê, bi taksiyê, bi peyatî); kîjan? and çiqas?; ya min, ya kê? (mine, whose?)
skills.grammarMd:
**Bi trênê diçim.** I go by train. *Bi* + a feminine noun with **-ê** says how you travel: *bi minîbûsê*, *bi taksiyê*, and on foot is **bi peyatî**.

- **Kîjan?** Which? *Kîjan kolan?* · **Çiqas?** How much, how far? *Çiqas dûr e?*
- **ya / yê** + owner: *Ev ya min e.* This is mine. · *Ya kê ye?* Whose is it?

lessons.beat: Hamo goes out early for bread to the bakery of his boyhood, where the old baker still remembers the boy who ate the crusts on the way home. The children argue about how you should all go back to Sêvan: by train, by plane, by taxi? Hevalo votes for going on foot, through every orchard on the way.

Packing: a mountain of shoes, bags and parcels by the door. Hamo sorts it all out: this bag is mine, that one is yours, and nothing at all belongs to Hevalo except the apples. In the street a man stops and stares: he knows Hamo, they were at school together, and they talk until Hamo’s mother phones to ask where he is, as she does every day.

new.en: whose; whom (kî after a preposition or a link)

lessons.beat: The last evening in Kobanî, and the news on the radio: snow is coming, and the mountain road may be closed by morning. You must go back tomorrow, early, while it is still open: by minibus, since there is no train and a taxi costs too much. Hamo sets three alarms, and asks you to check all of them.
Dawn, three alarms, and for once Hamo is on time. His mother fills every bag with bread and cheese, the children shout goodbye from the window, and the minibus climbs into the first snowflakes.

units.story: The minibus climbs the pass in the first snow, and Sêvan waits out the end of winter by the stove. Then the sun comes back, the snow melts, the stream by the walnut tree sings again, and the whole village gets ready for Newroz: Nazê sews new clothes, Baran gathers firewood, Xezo teaches the schoolchildren the steps of the govend, and Hamo practises a speech that the hens will not stay to hear. The future is on everyone’s lips (ez ê …, em ê …), and so is what everyone wants to do. On Newroz eve the neighbours come round with a lamp, for tea under a sky full of stars. By the fire on the hill everyone jumps over the flames and wishes each other health, Baran’s uncle plays the zurna, and when Hamo tries a shepherd’s flute, his first squeak makes the whole village laugh until they cry. The next morning, after a whole night of govend, Hamo cannot get out of bed. His back!

skills.grammar: the weather: baran dibare, berf dibare, ba tê, hewa sar e; the seasons bihar, havîn, payîz, zivistan
skills.grammarMd:
**Baran dibare.** It is raining (word for word: rain falls). Kurdish says what the weather does: **berf dibare** it is snowing, **ba tê** the wind is blowing, *hewa sar e* it is cold.

- **Baran** is rain, and it is also a boy’s name, like Nazê’s son.
- The seasons: *bihar* spring, *havîn* summer, *payîz* autumn, *zivistan* winter.
- “In winter” is **di zivistanê de**, or just **zivistanê**.

lessons.beat: The minibus climbs the pass in the first snow. Hamo, who has seen fifty winters, explains the weather to the driver as if the driver had never seen any: this is rain, that is snow, this is wind, and that sunshine through the clouds is a good sign, which the driver, who drives this road every day, already knew.

Snowed in at home, Hamo tells the children about the seasons of Sêvan, mostly about what you eat in each of them. Winter is for soup; spring is for the first roses; a sky with no clouds means the snow will melt soon. Hevalo presses his nose to the window and fogs it up, waiting for the warmth.

A storm rattles the shutters, and Hamo asks you about the weather where you come from: is summer hot there, is autumn wet, does it snow? Outside, Hevalo has made a snow-deer with an apple for a nose. He eats the nose.

The sun returns, the snow melts and the stream by the walnut tree sings again. Hamo goes over the whole winter with you, from the first snow to the storm, then phones every neighbour with the news: Newroz is coming!

skills.grammar: the future: ez ê, tu yê, ew ê, em ê, hûn ê + the bi- form (ez ê biçim, em ê bibînin); also dê (ez dê bêm)
skills.grammarMd:
**Ez ê biçim.** I will go. The future is the person, then **ê**, then the same bi- form as after *divê*: *tu yê bixwî*, *ew ê bê*, *em ê bibînin*.

- After a vowel *ê* becomes **yê**: *tu yê*. In many places people say **dê**: *Ez dê bêm.* I will come.
- *Sibe em ê êzing kom bikin.* Tomorrow we will gather firewood.

lessons.beat: Newroz is coming, and Hamo hands out the jobs: Baran will gather firewood for the fire, Nazê will sew new clothes for the children, Dapîr will bake, and he himself will… supervise. The preparations begin at once, mostly Hamo’s supervising, with tea.

The children count the days to Newroz on Dapîr’s calendar: fourteen, thirteen… Hamo is writing a speech for the fire, a great speech, which he will learn by heart afterwards. He dreams about it at night, a dream in which everyone claps. In the morning he cannot find it: has he forgotten where he put it? Bring it here, Hamo tells Hevalo, who is chewing something papery.

new.en: stayed, was left (past of mayîn; … roj ma ji … re: … days are left until …)

lessons.beat: Baran asks what Newroz really is. Hamo tells the old legend of Kawa the blacksmith, who lit fires on the hills to bring back the spring: the new year, the festival of a whole people. Since that day, he says, fires are lit on the hills every Newroz. The tale grows longer every year he tells it, and when you get up to go home, he starts it again from the beginning.

Hamo practises his Newroz speech in front of the hens. The hens leave. He practises in front of Bozo. Bozo leaves. He practises in front of you, and you stay to the end, so he gives it to you again, from the beginning.

skills.grammar: dixwazim with the bi- form (ez dixwazim govendê bigirim), and dixwazim ku … for someone else (ez dixwazim ku tu bêyî)
skills.grammarMd:
**Ez dixwazim govendê bigirim.** I want to dance (word for word: to hold the govend). After *dixwazim* the second verb takes the bi- form: *Ez dixwazim stranan bibêjim.* I want to sing songs.

- For someone else, add **ku** and their own form: *Ez dixwazim ku tu bêyî.* I want you to come.
- *Hamo dixwaze ku Baran êzing bîne.* Hamo wants Baran to bring firewood.

lessons.beat: At the school Xezo is teaching the children the govend steps for Newroz, and Hamo, passing by, tells you everything about it: who plays the drum, who plays the zurna, who leads with the handkerchief at the head of the line. The children sing a song. Hamo cannot resist joining the end of the line; three steps later he is in the middle of it, and the hens in the yard are dancing too, in their way.

new.en: to dance (word for word: to hold the govend)

lessons.beat: Nazê has sewn new clothes for everyone: a dress for Hêvî, new shoes for Baran, and for Hamo the traditional suit with a green sash, which he puts on straight away, over his pyjamas. The leader of the govend dances at the front, Hamo explains, and that will be him, if his knees agree.

new.en: leader of the govend (at the head of the line)

lessons.beat: The night before Newroz. Everything is ready; the forecast says rain, and Hamo says rain is a blessing. He asks you to look out with him: a full moon, and more stars than you have ever seen, as there always are in the village at night. Then a lamp at the blue gate: it is Nazê’s, and the neighbours have come for tea.

The neighbours are at the table, the new clothes are laid out, the firewood is stacked on the hill. Everybody says what they will do tomorrow, and Hamo says he will lead the govend, if his knees allow, and that they will.

skills.grammar: wishes with be (may it be): Newroza we pîroz be!, Destê te sax be!; the future and the bi- form at a celebration
skills.grammarMd:
**Newroza we pîroz be!** Happy Newroz to you all! **Be** is the bi- form of “to be”, and it makes a wish: *… pîroz be* may … be blessed.

- *Cejna te pîroz be!* Happy holiday! · *Destê te sax be!* Thank you for the food (may your hand be healthy).
- *Em ji te re tenduristî û serkeftin dixwazin.* We wish you health and success.

lessons.beat: Newroz morning: rain, then sun. The whole village climbs the hill for the picnic. At dusk Hamo lights the fire, and the young people jump over it one by one in the smoke, wishing each other health. Hamo jumps too, carefully, holding his moustache out of the way.

new.en: to light (a fire), to switch on

lessons.beat: By the dying fire Baran’s uncle plays the zurna and the children sing. Then Hamo takes out a shepherd’s flute: a terrible squeak, Hevalo bolts, and everyone laughs until tears of joy come. This is life, Hamo tells you, wiping his eyes, and he wishes everyone health and success in the new year.

new.en: continuously, on and on (berdewam kirin: to go on, to continue)

lessons.beat: The next morning, after a whole night of govend, Hamo cannot get out of bed. “Pişta min diêşe!” Where is the pain? Everywhere. Is it bad? Very bad, he says, and asks you for tea, honey and sympathy, in that order.

Hamo, from his bed, tells everyone who comes to see him about Newroz: the fire, the flute, the govend, the speech nobody heard. Nazê phones to ask about his back; he says it is a little better, which is almost true.

units.story: After all that govend Hamo’s back has given up, and he turns out to be the most dramatic patient in the valley. The neighbours fuss, Nazê brings soup, and the doctor who comes up from the town, Doctor Azad, an old man with a kind voice and no patience for nonsense, examines Hamo from top to toe. Body words, aches and feelings, the doctor’s questions (“Tu min dibînî? Li ku diêşe?”), and, once Hamo is back on his feet, a moustache contest at the tea house, with comparisons and superlatives flying. Honey is forbidden; a jar goes missing; a moustache is sticky. Then Baran, the neighbours’ boy, comes home late one evening, muddy and silent, and will not say what happened, and Hamo learns to listen.

skills.grammar: what hurts: … min diêşe (serê min diêşe), … min diêşin for more than one (lingên min diêşin)
skills.grammarMd:
**Serê min diêşe.** My head hurts. The part of the body comes first, with its link and its owner, then **diêşe**: *pişta min diêşe*, *milê wî diêşe*.

- For more than one, **diêşin**: *Lingên min diêşin.* My legs hurt.
- *Ez nexweş im.* I’m ill. · *Ez westiyayî me.* I’m tired. · *Tu sax î?* Are you well?

lessons.beat: Hamo lies in bed and lists every part of himself that hurts, from his legs to his shoulders and back again. He is ill, he says, and tired, and in need of medicine, and of tea. Nazê tells him to rest; Hamo says he has been resting since breakfast and it is exhausting.

Nazê asks where exactly it hurts. Everywhere, says Hamo: his neck, his little finger, and now he has a cough, and probably a fever. He is sad about it, very sad, until someone says the doctor is coming from the town; then he hides the honey under the bedding and looks almost cheerful.

new.en: glad, pleased, happy (people also say kêfxweş)

lessons.beat: Doctor Azad arrives with his old leather bag. Does Hamo need the hospital in the town? Hamo sits up at once: he does not want to go! Then his tooth hurts, and his chest, and his whole body, so that he cannot get up, and while the doctor listens to his chest, Hamo talks and talks, and the doctor waits, very patiently, for him to stop.

The neighbours visit one by one, and each asks Hamo what hurts. Each gets a different answer, and a longer one. Doctor Azad listens to all of them from the doorway, says that the only thing really wrong with Hamo is his patience, and leaves him some medicine.

skills.grammar: pronouns as objects in the present, before the verb (doktor min dibîne, ez te dibînim); jê for ji + him, her, it
skills.grammarMd:
**Doktor min dibîne.** The doctor sees me. A pronoun as the object goes before the verb, in its other form, the one you know from *navê min*: *min, te, wî, wê, me, we, wan*: *Ez te dibînim.* I see you. · *Tu wî nas dikî?* Do you know him?

- **jê** is *ji* + him, her or it: *Ez jê hez dikim.* I like it. · *Jê bipirse!* Ask him!

lessons.beat: Doctor Azad examines Hamo from top to toe: he listens to his heart, which beats like a drum, presses his back and frowns. Hamo asks for pills, please, not an injection; he is afraid of the needle, but only a little. The doctor laughs: Hamo will be better in a week, if he does exactly as he is told.

new.en: to beat (of the heart); to hit
to listen (guhdariya … kirin: to listen to)

lessons.beat: The doctor’s advice: rest, walk a little every day, and no honey at night: honey is forbidden. Hamo says he is not weak, he is strong, and will walk to the mountain by Friday. Then the neighbours come to visit, each one bringing… a jar of honey. The doctor takes every jar from them and gives them to you to guard, because he knows Hamo.

new.en: from him, from her, from it (ji + wî/wê)

lessons.beat: You and Hevalo guard the honey all night. In the morning one jar is empty, and Hamo’s moustache is suspiciously sticky. Who is the thief? Hamo says he is innocent, completely innocent, and asks you whether you believe him. Hevalo, for once, really is innocent, and looks offended.

The honey case is closed: the doctor finds a sticky spoon under Hamo’s pillow. Hamo says it is a very clever thief who leaves the spoon with someone else. Everyone laughs, and the doctor takes the last jar home, for safety.

skills.grammar: comparing with -tir and ji (Baran ji Hêviyê mezintir e); the most with herî (simbêlê herî dirêj, ya herî baş); baş → çêtir
skills.grammarMd:
**Baran ji Hêviyê mezintir e.** Baran is older than Hêvî. Add **-tir** to the adjective and put **ji** before what you compare with: *dirêjtir* longer, *kintir* shorter.

- The most is **herî** before the adjective: *simbêlê herî dirêj* the longest moustache · *ya herî baş* the best one.
- *baş* good has its own word for better: **çêtir**.

lessons.beat: Back on his feet, Hamo compares everyone in the house and the lane: who is taller, older, cleverer. Baran is older than Hêvî; the girl next door is sixteen and her brother seventeen, no, the other way round, and Hamo goes round to ask. He himself, he says, is the cleverest of all, and his moustache the longest, though his patience is a little short.

Hamo asks everyone their favourites: the best season, the sweetest fruit, the most beautiful place in the world. Everyone chooses something different; Hevalo’s answer to every question is the same. Hamo’s favourite tea glass is special: it is the biggest of all and holds more sugar, and Sêvan’s apples, he says, are famous all the way to Kobanî.

The village moustache contest at the tea house, with Doctor Azad as judge. Hamo is sure he will win. Ferhad’s moustache is longer. Hamo’s, he announces, is the most beautiful, and the room agrees, laughing; he graciously promises Ferhad the prize next year, and asks you who you think really won.

Hamo is better, and walks every day with you and Hevalo. Who walks fastest? Hevalo. Who walks slowest? Hamo, who stops to talk to everyone. The best medicine, Hamo says, is the air of the mountains, and the second best is tea.

skills.grammar: feelings in the present (ez ditirsim, ez dihizirim, ez tê digihîjim); xwe for oneself (ew li xwe dinêre); guhdariya min bike
skills.grammarMd:
**Ez ditirsim.** I’m afraid. Kurdish says this with a verb, *ditirsim* (word for word: I fear), where English uses an adjective. *Dihizirim* I think and *tê digihîjim* I understand are verbs too; *tê digihîjim* comes in two pieces.

- **xwe** is oneself, whoever that is: *Ez li xwe dinêrim.* I look at myself. · *Ew li xwe dinêre.* He looks at himself.
- **Guhdariya min bike!** Listen to me! (word for word: do my listening)

lessons.beat: Baran comes home late one evening, muddy to the knees, and will not say a word. Hamo asks you what you think it is: anger? shame? He is not calm, that much is clear. Hêvî is amazed: her brother, quiet! Hamo has a feeling about it, and he is in no hurry to find out; he wants to wait.

Baran sits alone on the flat roof. Hamo climbs up, slowly, his back complaining at every rung, and sits beside him without a word. Then he talks quietly: about trust, about how a secret is heavy to carry alone and lighter when you share it, about the truth being better than a lie, even a small one. Baran listens.

new.en: to understand (li … tê gihîştin: to understand someone)

lessons.beat: By the stove Hamo tells a story from his childhood: at eight he lost the neighbour’s best ram in the melting snow and hid behind a rock all day, afraid to go home, a coward, he thought. In the evening he told the neighbour the truth, and the neighbour called him honest and brave. (The ram came home by itself.) Brave people, you tell Hamo, are the ones who tell the truth.

Baran comes down from the roof and sits by the stove. He does not tell yet; he says “Sibe ez ê bibêjim.” Then Hevalo sits next to him and offers him his last apple, and that, everyone agrees, is a very big moment.

units.story: At breakfast Baran finally tells what happened yesterday: he took Bozo to the river, Bozo saw a goat across the valley and ran off, Baran ran after him, got lost among the rocks, sat down under a walnut tree and fell asleep, and came home in the dark by the stars, to find that Bozo had been home for hours, eating Dapîr’s mint. Then everyone tells their own yesterday, and the days of long ago: Hamo as a handsome young man with a black moustache, the wolves that roam around the village when it gets dark and the bears and foxes of the forest, and Dapîr’s summers on the pastures as a girl. A message comes down from Bişar the shepherd: something wild and shy, like a deer, comes to his tent every night. Hevalo’s ears go straight up, and Hamo decides that this summer everyone goes up to the zozan. Then Bozo runs away again, and is found at the spring with Ferhad’s little donkey, very much in love.

skills.grammar: the past of verbs without an object: past stem + -im, -î, —, -in (ez çûm, tu hatî, ew ket, em man); ne- for not (neçûm)
skills.grammarMd:
**Ez duh çûm çem.** Yesterday I went to the river. Verbs like *çûn* go, *hatin* come and *ketin* fall use their past stem with the endings **-im, -î, —, -in**: *ez çûm, tu çûyî, ew çû, em çûn*.

- *ez hatim, ew hat* · *ez ketim, ew ket* · *ez mam, ew ma* (stayed)
- “Didn’t” is **ne-** in front: *ez neçûm*, *ew nehat*.

lessons.beat: At breakfast Baran takes a deep breath: “Duh ez çûm çem…” The whole table goes quiet; even the kettle seems to stop. He was by the river with Bozo, and suddenly something happened. Hamo, who fell into that same river last year, nods gravely: it has happened before.

Baran goes on: Bozo saw a goat on the other side of the valley and ran. Baran ran after him, over the stones, along the cliffs and in among the trees, and never reached him. He was left all alone. Hamo asks you to guess what happened next.

You ask the questions everyone is afraid to ask, and Hamo answers for Baran: he was a little afraid; he sat down under a walnut tree to think, and fell asleep. When he got up, it was dark. And Hamo himself, under a tree? He would eat some walnuts first.

When Baran woke it was dark, so he followed the stars home, as Hamo once taught him. And Bozo? Bozo had come home by himself hours before, and eaten all of Dapîr’s mint. Everyone laughs, Baran hardest of all. But he saw something on the way: smoke from a tent where nobody lives.

skills.grammar: time in the past: duh, pêr, par, berê, hefteya borî; dema ku … (when …) with the past
skills.grammarMd:
**Dema ku ez zarok bûm, …** When I was a child, … *Dema ku* (when) sets the time something happens, and what happened then follows; *ku* is often left out: *Dema ku ez vegeriyam, ew li malê bû.* When I came back, he was at home.

- *duh* yesterday · *pêr* the day before yesterday · *par* last year · *berê* before, in the old days · *hefteya borî* last week

lessons.beat: Hamo sits back, strokes his moustache and begins the old days: when he was a boy in Kobanî, and when he was a handsome young man in the traditional suit, with a moustache as black as the night. Last week Dapîr was ill, and now she is better; the day before yesterday Bozo ran away, again; and on long summer nights, when the stars came out, everyone came home happy. Nazê pours more tea: this will take a while. Dapîr says that when she was young the summers were longer; Hamo says they were the same length, only with fewer clocks.

new.en: went out, came out (past of derketin)

lessons.beat: Hamo tells you about the animals of the hills. When it gets dark, wolves roam around the village; bears and wolves live in the forest, where it is dark even at noon; and once, when the children sat around the fire, a fox came out of the trees to look at them. And the big wolf everyone saw at the gate one winter night? It wasn’t a wolf at all: it was the neighbours’ dog. Hêvî laughs until she has to sit down.

A boy on a mule brings a message down from the pastures, from Bişar the shepherd: something wild comes to his tent every night, shy as a shadow, like a deer. Hevalo’s ears shoot straight up. Hamo reads the message to you twice, and asks you what you think it is.

Everyone tells a story from when they were small, each with a different animal in it: a wolf at the gate, a bear in the forest, Hêvî’s clever fox. The best story, everyone agrees, is Dapîr’s, because it is true: the year she found a lamb in the snow and carried it home under her shawl.

skills.grammar: telling events in order: pêşî, paşê, piştre, di dawiyê de; piştî ku … (after …) with the past, berî ku … (before …) with the bi- form
skills.grammarMd:
**Pêşî em rabûn, paşê em çûn.** First we got up, then we went. *Pêşî*, *paşê*, *piştre* and **di dawiyê de** (in the end) put a story in order.

- **piştî ku** + the past: *Piştî ku em gihîştin, em rûniştin.* After we arrived, we sat down.
- **berî ku** + the bi- form: *Berî ku em biçin, divê em çay vexwin.* Before we go, we must drink tea.

lessons.beat: Hamo teaches Baran how to tell a story properly, first, then, in the end: first we went to the market, then to the river, and in the end we came home; in July we went up the mountain, and in August we came back. Baran wants to get to the end at once. Be patient, says Hamo: first tea, then the story. A good story, he says, is like tea: it needs time.

Hamo retells Baran’s day in order, and it becomes a hero’s journey: Baran walked, wandered, stopped, laughed at his fear, and slept like a shepherd under the stars, all on his own. A bird flew over him, says Hamo, an eagle, probably. Baran agrees that it was probably an eagle. Dapîr, who worked all day, says it was a crow.

Hamo makes a decision: this summer everyone, the neighbours, Dapîr and you, will move up to the zozan, to Bişar’s tent, to see his mysterious visitor. In summer the village is hot, he says, but up on the pastures the weather is lovely. He asks you whether you have ever slept in a tent. The packing begins at once, and Bozo, hearing the word “zozan”, runs away again.

new.en: to move house, to migrate (with the flocks)

lessons.beat: Packing for the zozan: tents, ropes, pots, Dapîr’s saddlebags and four sacks of apples, which Hamo says are for Bişar and Hevalo says nothing about. Everyone tells what they did today, in order, and Hamo’s day is the shortest: he sat, he drank tea, he slept.

skills.grammar: a story in the past: hebû and tunebû (there was, there wasn’t), the negative past (neçû, nehat, nebû)
skills.grammarMd:
**Hespekî me hebû.** We had a horse. *Heye* in the past is **hebû**, and *tune* is **tunebû**: *Li wir dibistan tunebû.* There was no school there.

- The past with **ne-**: *Ez neçûm dibistanê.* I didn’t go to school. · *Ew nehat.* He didn’t come.
- For more than one, “there were” is *hebûn*.

lessons.beat: Dapîr, packing her old saddlebags, tells what she did at Baran’s age: her family had a horse, and every summer they rode up to the pastures; she climbed the hills faster than the boys and came down the other side singing. At fifteen she could carry a lamb; at eighteen, two. There was no school up there, but there was everything else.

new.en: there was; (someone) had (the past of heye)
to go down, to get off

lessons.beat: Hamo tells how organised the family will be this time, and how, the last time they moved to the pastures, he was late by one whole day: by mistake, of course, completely by mistake. A small mistake. This time everyone leaves at dawn, he says, and he will be wide awake. He tests the ropes for the packs. Bozo watches, shy, from behind the wall: Bozo has been acting strangely all week.

Bozo has run away again! You and Baran follow his tracks up the valley while Hamo calls his name and Hevalo leads the way. You find him at the spring with Ferhad’s little donkey, the two of them very much in love. “Bozo evîndar e!” says Hamo, delighted, and then, solemnly, “Evîn nehênî ye,” and he begs you not to tell Ferhad.

On the climb Dapîr shows you the places she remembers, the rock where they stopped to rest, the spring where she filled her jug, and tells what was here then and what is not now. Hamo listens, for once, without a word. Bozo walks very slowly and keeps looking back. Then a flock of sheep fills the path, and a voice calls Hamo’s name.

units.story: The shepherd on the path is Bişar, Hamo’s old friend, and he leads everyone up to the zozan, the high summer pastures, where his black tents stand by a cold spring. Life up there is milk and bread and work: milking at dawn, churning butter in a goatskin, baking bread on the saj, songs at night under more stars than Baran can count. The mysterious visitor is Zerê, a shy wild doe who comes every night for the salt Bişar puts out, and from the moment Hevalo sees her he has eyes for nobody else: he brings her apples, he forgets his own, and one morning he is gone with the whole sack. Following the two deer, the camp finds a hidden lake and an old stone house: Dapîr’s summer home when she was a girl, where, she remembers, a young flute player from Kobanî used to play for the shepherds by the lake. You learn the past of verbs that take an object (min nan xwar, te çi dît?) and the past continuous for the old summers. At the end of the summer Hevalo says a long goodbye to Zerê, and everyone goes back down to the village with a notebook full of stories.

skills.grammar: the past of verbs with an object is ergative: the doer is min, te, wî, wê, me, we, wan, and the verb takes its past stem (min nan xwar, te çi kir?)
skills.grammarMd:
**Min nan xwar.** I ate bread. With a verb that has an object, the past works differently: the doer is **min, te, wî, wê, me, we, wan**, not *ez, tu*, and the verb uses its past stem: *Te çi kir?* What did you do? · *Wî got …* He said …

- *xwarin* → *xwar* · *vexwarin* → *vexwar* · *kirin* → *kir* · *gotin* → *got* · *dîtin* → *dît*
- *Me çay vexwar.* We drank tea.

lessons.beat: The shepherd on the path is Bişar, Hamo’s old friend. They drink tea on the rocks while his flock goes past, and Hamo tells him everything that happened on the way up, twice. Bişar picks up Dapîr’s bag, puts it down in front of his tent and asks what you saw, what you ate, what Bozo did. Hamo gets as far as “Me çay vexwar…”

At the tents Bişar asks everyone what they saw on the climb. Baran saw an eagle; Hêvî a hundred flowers in the meadow; Hamo saw nothing, because he was talking. Who brought the bread? Who took the tea glasses? Bozo wanted the grass and nothing else, and nobody heard a word Hamo said after that, because the sheep were louder.

At dusk you and Hamo see her at the edge of the meadow: a doe, licking the salt that Bişar puts out every night. She stops and looks straight at Hevalo, and Hevalo drops his apple. “Bêdeng!” whispers Hamo. Bişar says he once tried to catch her and caught only his own hat; Hamo leaves a sack of apples by the tent and asks you to keep very still.

By the fire Bişar tells how the doe comes every night for the salt, and Hamo names her Zerê, “the golden one”. Everyone says what they did today; Hamo did a great deal, he says, and Bişar says he saw him do none of it. In the morning Hevalo is gone, and so is the sack of apples.

skills.grammar: in the ergative past the verb agrees with the object: min sêvek xwar (one apple), min sêv xwarin (apples); min tu dîtî (I saw you)
skills.grammarMd:
**Min sêv xwarin.** I ate apples. In this past, with *min, te, wî*…, the verb agrees with the **thing done**, not the doer: *min sêvek xwar* (one apple) but *min sêv xwarin* (apples). Here *xwarin* is “ate”, for more than one thing, not “to eat”.

- With a pronoun as the object it shows the person: *Min tu dîtî.* I saw you. · *Te ez dîtim.* You saw me. · *Me hûn dîtin.* We saw you all.
- So *Wî ez dîtim* is “he saw me”, and *Min ew dît* is “I saw him”.

lessons.beat: Dawn on the zozan: Bişar teaches you to milk a ewe, and Dapîr shows Nazê how her mother made butter in a goatskin churn, rocking it until only the ayran is left. Hamo milks one ewe, proudly, and spills half of it. Then dough is made from flour and water for the bread on the saj, and Hamo says he will make the best bread on the mountain.

Dapîr and Nazê cook bread on the saj over the fire, each one thin as paper. Hamo “helps” and burns one; Bişar teases him for an hour. Baran washed the glasses at the spring, Hêvî read her book, and Hamo wrote in his notebook: “I made bread today.” Then you see Hevalo slipping away to the meadow with an apple in his mouth. “Min tu dîtî!” He pretends he did not see you see him.

The whole camp follows the tracks of the two deer up the valley, and high above the tents you find a lake nobody has seen for fifty years: Hevalo and Zerê on the shore, sharing apples. Beside the lake stands an old stone house, half in ruins. Who was its owner? Hamo takes out his phone for a photo, and asks you to guess.

new.en: to take out, to bring out

lessons.beat: Back at the tents everyone tells what they saw at the lake: the two deer, the stone house, water so clear you could see the fish. Hamo saw it all first, he says. Bişar saw Hamo arrive last. They argue happily all evening, and Hevalo, who only has eyes for Zerê, falls asleep dreaming of her.

skills.titleEn: I was eating, I was going
skills.grammar: the past continuous: di- + the past stem, for what used to happen or was happening (ez diçûm, min dixwar, wan digot)
skills.grammarMd:
**Em her havîn diçûn zozanan.** We used to go to the pastures every summer. **di-** + the past stem says what used to happen, or what was going on: *ez diçûm* I used to go, *ew dihat* she used to come.

- With a verb that has an object it works like the simple past: *min dixwar* I used to eat, *wan digot* they used to say.
- *Dema ku min çay vedixwar, …* While I was drinking tea, …

lessons.beat: At the old stone house Dapîr stops at the door. This was her family’s summer home: in those days they used to come up from the plain every summer, it was the custom, and she used to swim in the lake every afternoon, dry curd on that very roof and look after the lambs, all day long, from morning to night.

new.en: was …-ing, used to (the past continuous: diçûm, min dixwar)

lessons.beat: Dapîr tells: when she was a girl, the women used to milk while the girls sang, and at night the whole household slept on felt rugs by the fire, even when lightning lit the sky. Her mother used to sing her a lullaby; she came up here nineteen summers in a row. And every evening a young man from Kobanî used to play the flute for the shepherds by the lake. Dapîr still remembers the tune, and hums it for you.

The last days on the zozan. Hevalo goes up to the lake to say goodbye to Zerê; she nudges an apple back towards him, and then she is gone into the grass. He comes back sad and eats only two apples. Everyone packs with a heavy heart; Bişar promises a meeting next summer, and Hamo asks you whether you will come back up with them.

lessons.titleKu: Dema ku em li vir bûn
lessons.beat: On the last evening Dapîr hums the tune the flute player used to play by the lake, and Bişar remembers his own father dancing to it. Hamo tells what the old shepherds used to say about these mountains, and the fire burns low while the old summers come back one by one.

skills.grammar: telling a whole day in the past, mixing both kinds of verb (ez çûm û min … dît); questions in the past (te çi kir?, kê got?, çi qewimî?)
skills.grammarMd:
