**Ez çûm golê û min ask dîtin.** I went to the lake and I saw deer. A story mixes both kinds of past: *ez çûm*, *ez hatim* with a verb that has no object, *min dît*, *min got* with one that has.

- Questions keep the same order: *Te çi kir?* What did you do? · *Kê got?* Who said it? · *Çi qewimî?* What happened?
- *ji … re gotin* to tell someone: *Min ji te re got!* I told you!

lessons.beat: Back in Sêvan, everyone tells the summer at once. The neighbours who stayed behind ask what happened. Baran tells the whole journey as a great adventure; Hêvî shows the flowers she pressed; Hamo shows the photos he took, mostly of his own finger. The biggest event, everyone agrees, was the lake, and Hevalo’s face whenever someone says “Zerê”.

Who saw the lake first? Who burned the bread? Who said the doe was “just a goat”? Hamo says he does not remember saying that; Baran shouts that he did; Hamo is astonished. “We had a summer like no other,” he says, to change the subject: worth every step of the climb. Everyone is happy to agree.

Hamo writes the summer down in his old notebook, slowly, so that nothing is lost: everything important, and some things that aren’t. He is a little worried: the apples are nearly ripe, school starts soon, and the harvest needs every pair of hands. His hope? A good harvest, and you to help with it. He asks if you will stay.

Hamo reads the summer aloud from his notebook, from the first glass of tea on the rocks to Hevalo’s last goodbye at the lake, and everyone corrects him: it was he, not Bişar, who burned the bread. Hamo crosses it out and writes it again his way, because it is a better story.

units.story: Autumn in Sêvan: the apples are ripe, school has started, and everybody in the village has a trade, and an opinion about everyone else’s. Ferhad farms, Mîrza sells, Bişar keeps sheep, the builder mends the mill, and Hamo, of course, is in charge of tea. Then news comes: a school in Hewlêr, far away, has offered Xezo, the village teacher, a post. The whole village comes to help with the apple harvest behind the blue gate, and at the village meeting afterwards Xezo says she has decided: she will go after the winter, and come back for every Newroz. The present perfect says what has been done (me sêv berhev kirine, wê biryar daye) and the linking words say why (ji ber ku, loma, lê, hem … hem). Baran has to give a talk about Sêvan in front of the whole school and is terrified; Hamo helps him write it, and the hens hear it first. Everyone talks about plans and hopes, yours too: what you will do with your Kurdish, and who you will speak it with. As the first snow comes, Hamo promises a tale by the stove every winter night.

skills.grammar: jobs and the endings that make them: -kar (cotkar), -ker (karker), -dar (dikandar), -pêj (nanpêj); bûn for becoming (ez ê bibim mamoste)
skills.grammarMd:
**Karê te çi ye?** What’s your job? — **Ez cotkar im.** I’m a farmer. Many job names are a word plus an ending: *kar* work → **karker** worker, *dikan* shop → **dikandar** shopkeeper, *nan* bread → **nanpêj** baker.

- To become is *bûn*: *Ez dixwazim bibim mamoste.* I want to become a teacher. · *Ew ê bibe nivîskar.* He will become a writer.

lessons.beat: September, and the apples are nearly ripe. Hamo walks you through the village trades: Ferhad the farmer on his tractor, the shopkeeper who opens when he feels like it, the cook at the tea house, the builder who mended the mill, the workers from the town who come for the harvest. Every trade, says Hamo, is the best one, according to the person who does it. By October the apples must be in.

The children play “what will you be?”. Baran will be a writer of adventures; Hêvî a nurse for the hens; the neighbour’s eldest son, a translator. Hamo says he would have been an artist, which is the same as a writer with more tea. Meanwhile someone must plant the new saplings in the soil, and he looks at you.

News in the village: a school in Hewlêr has offered Xezo, the village teacher, a post, a big school in a big city, far away. Hamo passes the news on to you over tea: “Ev derfeteke mezin e!” It is an honour for Sêvan, he says; but Hewlêr is far, and the children will miss their teacher. He asks you what you would do.

Hamo works in the orchard all day, and the village stops by one after another (Ferhad, Mîrza, Bişar down from the pastures), each telling him why his own work is the best in the world. Hamo listens to them all, agrees with each, and then asks you which job you would choose.

skills.grammar: the present perfect: past stem + -ime, -iyî, -iye, -ine, after a vowel -me, -yî, -ye, -ne (ez hatime, ew çûye); ergative with an object (min kiriye)
skills.grammarMd:
**Ez hatime.** I have come. The present perfect is the past stem + **-ime, -iyî, -iye, -ine** after a consonant, **-me, -yî, -ye, -ne** after a vowel: *ew hatiye* he has come, *em çûne* we have gone.

- With a verb that has an object it works like the past, with *min, te, wî*… as the doer: *Min biryar daye.* I have decided. · *Me sêv berhev kirine.* We have picked the apples.
- *Te hîç Amed dîtiye?* Have you ever seen Amed?

lessons.beat: The harvest begins. Hamo has an idea: this year he will change everything, ladders on the left, baskets on the right, tea in the middle. He has slept on it twice, he says, and he is satisfied. The field below the orchard is done by noon, the trees will be by Friday, unless the work finishes the workers first. Dapîr, who has the most experience, says nothing and keeps picking.

new.en: has …ed (the present perfect: hatiye, min kiriye)

lessons.beat: Everyone picks: the children the low branches, Hamo the high ones, singing from the top of a ladder. The crates fill up, the load on Bozo grows heavy, and Bozo sits down. The baskets are light, says Hamo; it is Bozo who is heavy-hearted. Then a cloud comes over the mountain, and everyone works in a hurry.

new.en: to gather, to pick (fruit, the harvest)

lessons.beat: After the harvest, a meeting in the square: the apples are shared, a basket for every house and the first for the school. Then Xezo stands up and tells the village what she has decided: she will take the post in Hewlêr after the winter, and come back for every Newroz. Hamo tells you what everyone said: Dapîr, that a brave choice is never a wrong one; Baran, nothing at all. November is coming, and the first frost.

lessons.titleKu: Ez ê biçim, lê ez ê vegerim
lessons.titleEn: I’ll go, but I’ll come back
lessons.beat: Xezo has written to the school in Hewlêr: yes, she will come in the spring. The whole village knows by lunchtime, because Mîrza took the letter to the post. Then Baran comes to Hamo with a problem of his own: his teacher wants him to give a talk about the village in front of the whole school, and he is terrified.

skills.grammar: linking ideas: ji ber ku and çimkî (because), loma and ji ber vê yekê (so), lê and lêbelê (but), hem … hem (both … and), bêyî ku (without)
skills.grammarMd:
**Ez dibezim, ji ber ku ez dereng im.** I’m running because I’m late. **ji ber ku** and **çimkî** say why; **loma** and **ji ber vê yekê** say what follows: *Baran ditirse, loma ew bêdeng e.* Baran is afraid, so he is quiet.

- **lê** and **lêbelê** but, however · **hem … hem** both … and: *hem sêv hem tirî*
- **bêyî ku** + the bi- form: *bêyî ku tiştekî bibêje* without saying anything

lessons.beat: Xezo has given Baran’s class a task before she goes: each child will give a talk about their village in front of the whole school, and Baran’s subject is Sêvan. Baran explains to Hamo why he can’t: because he is shy, because his voice shakes, which is to say, he would rather not. That is why, says Hamo, they will practise, and also drink tea.

Baran lists the reasons he cannot do it: the hall is big, the children will laugh, his voice will shake. Hamo answers every “lê” with a “lêbelê”: the hall is big, but the children are his friends; his voice will shake, but voices do that. In short, Baran will speak both loudly and slowly, just as Hamo does in his speeches. That, says Baran, is clearly what he is afraid of.

Hamo helps Baran write his talk, letter by letter, full of becauses and so’s. Baran practises in front of the hens, as Hamo once did, and Hevalo, the most patient listener in the world, stays to the end and stamps a hoof by way of applause. Hamo asks you to listen too and to tell Baran honestly how it was. Baran will try, he says, and that is all anyone can do.

Baran gives his talk in the school hall: Sêvan, because it has the best apples; its people, because they help each other; and Hevalo, because he is Hevalo. The whole school claps. Xezo, his teacher, says it was the best talk of the year, and Baran is so happy that he gives it again at home, twice.

skills.grammar: plans and hopes: hêvî dikim ku … and armanca min ev e ku … + the bi- form; dema ku … + the bi- form for the future (dema ku ez vegerim malê, …)
skills.grammarMd:
**Hêvî dikim ku tu bêyî.** I hope you’ll come. After **hêvî dikim ku** (I hope that) and **armanca min ev e ku** (my aim is to) the verb takes the bi- form.

- **dema ku** + the bi- form looks ahead: *Dema ku ez vegerim malê, ez ê bi kurdî biaxivim.* When I go back home, I’ll speak Kurdish.
- With the past, **dema ku** looks back: *Dema ku ez hatim Sêvanê, …* When I came to Sêvan, …
- *Armanca min ev e ku ez her roj hinek bixwînim.* My aim is to read a little every day.

lessons.beat: Baran’s talk was a success, and now he wants to give another (!). Hamo asks everyone about their goals: Hêvî wants a cat, Nazê wants Hamo to be on time once, and Hamo wants a good harvest every year and a new tea glass. Then he asks about your plan: what will you do with your Kurdish? All learning, he says, is one step at a time, and you have already come a long way.

The children tell Hamo all about Xezo’s plans for Hewlêr: a small room near the school, a phone call home every Friday, and her mother tongue taught to children every day. Then Hamo asks about you: your country, your place in the world, who will hear your Kurdish first. Does a person forget their roots far away? Not Hamo, whose roots are still in Kobanî: in his first winter here he was homesick, and the village gave him strength and warmth.

new.en: to be homesick (word for word: to miss home)

lessons.beat: The first snow. Hamo lights the stove and makes a plan of his own: a winter evening of tales every night at the blue gate, one of Dapîr’s old tales each time. Dapîr is the village’s storyteller, he says, and he is trying to become one too. And there is news from Mîrza: a dengbêj is travelling the villages this winter. Hamo asks you which you like better, a tale or a song.

new.en: a winter evening of stories and visits
dengbêj, the traditional singer of tales

lessons.beat: The last winter before Xezo leaves, and snow on every roof. Hamo sums up the autumn: what everyone has done, what everyone hopes, why it was a good year. Then he opens the stove door, puts the kettle on, and begins the first tale of the winter, for the children and for you: “Hebû tunebû…”

units.story: The last winter by the stove. Each night Hamo tells one of the old tales (Şengê and Pengê and the wolf at the door, the fox who shared a field with the bear) while Dapîr answers every tale with a proverb and the children act them out; Hevalo makes a terrible wolf, far too friendly. One snowy night travellers knock: an old dengbêj and his grandson, who sing for their supper, and their kilam about a shepherd who played the flute by a lake is missing its last verse, which nobody remembers. Conditions (heke tu derî vekî …) and reported speech (wî got ku …) join everything the road has taught. Spring comes, and with it Ferhad’s son’s wedding, which is also the village’s farewell to its teacher: Xezo thanks everyone for every tale and every glass of tea, and at dawn the bus takes her from the blue gate to Hewlêr. Then the village turns to you, at the blue gate where your road began: “Rêya te vekirî be!”

skills.grammar: conditions: heke / eger + the bi- form (heke tu derî vekî, gur tê); the bi- form of “to be”: bim, bî, be, bin (heke tu birçî bî)
skills.grammarMd:
**Heke tu derî vekî, gur tê.** If you open the door, the wolf will come in. After **heke** or **eger** (if) the verb takes the bi- form; what follows is in the present or the future.

- The bi- form of “to be” is **bim, bî, be, bin**: *Heke tu birçî bî, bixwe!* If you’re hungry, eat!
- *Eger baran bibare, em ê li malê bimînin.* If it rains, we’ll stay at home.

lessons.beat: Hamo begins the first tale: a mother goat goes up to the pastures each morning and tells her two kids, Şengê and Pengê, never to open the door to anyone, if anyone knocks, if anyone sings. But the wolf is a liar: he makes his voice as soft as wool to trick the kids. Hêvî hides her face in Dapîr’s shawl.

The wolf knocks at the door and sings like their mother. Hamo stops to ask the children: what will happen if they open the door? Şengê sees through the trick: the voice is sweet, but under the door are grey paws. Good sense and cleverness, says Hamo, are worth more than strong legs, and Baran says that if he were the kid he would have opened the door, just to see the wolf.

new.en: (that I) be; (if) I am: the bi- form of “to be”

lessons.beat: The children turn the tale into a play by the stove. Everyone wants a part; Hevalo gets the wolf and plays it terribly, far too friendly, and he keeps pushing apples under the door with his hoof. Hamo directs the play from his cushion and asks you to be the mother goat, since nobody else will.
Dapîr says every tale has a lesson, and gives one for this one. Baran asks for another story. Then a loud knock at the door, in the middle of a snowy night.

skills.grammar: reported speech: got ku … (he said that …), pirsî ka … (he asked whether …), dibêjin ku … (they say that …); gelo? (I wonder)
skills.grammarMd:
**Wî got ku ew birçî ye.** He said he was hungry. Kurdish reports speech with **ku** and keeps the speaker’s own tense: *Wî got ku ew ê bê.* He said he would come.

- A question is reported with **ka**: *Wê pirsî ka tu kengî têyî.* She asked when you were coming.
- **gelo** I wonder: *Gelo ew kî ne?* I wonder who they are.

lessons.beat: December, deep snow, and a knock at midnight: an old dengbêj and his grandson, caught by the storm. Hamo does not ask who they are, “Bi xêr hatin! Werin hundir!”, and spreads the meal cloth at once: hospitality asks no questions until the guests have eaten. The old man thanks him, “Mala te ava! Xwedê ji te razî be!”, and says Sêvan is the most hospitable village in the mountains. Hamo pretends not to be pleased.

new.en: Thank you! (may God be pleased with you)
the cloth a meal is laid on; a meal spread

lessons.beat: Over dinner everyone talks at once, and Hamo passes it all on: the old man said that the pass will be closed until February, the grandson asked whether there were apples, Dapîr asked whether they knew her cousin, Baran complains that nobody listens to him. Then another knock: who can that be, Hamo wonders, in this snow? If the pass opens in January, he promises, he will let everyone know.

After dinner the old man sings: kilams of the old days in a voice that fills the house, each tune rising and falling like the mountain road. He has the finest voice Hamo has ever heard, and his last kilam is about a shepherd who played the flute by a lake on the pastures. But its last verse is lost, and nobody knows it. Hamo wonders aloud who could still know it, and you think of Dapîr.
In the morning Hamo phones the town to ask whether the pass is open: no answer. When the snow stops, the guests go on their way, leaving the song unfinished, and the whole village hums it for days.

skills.grammar: proverbs and how they are built: the plain present for what is always true (… dibe, … derdixe), and … çiqas … be (however … may be)
skills.grammarMd:
**Av dilop dilop dibe gol.** Drop by drop, water becomes a lake. Proverbs speak in the plain present, because they are true every day: *dibe* becomes, *derdixe* brings out.

- **çiqas … be** however … it may be (often with **jî**: *çiqas bilind be jî*): *Çiya çiqas bilind be, wê rê pê keve.* However high the mountain, a road will cross it. Here **wê** is another way to say **dê**, will.
- *Mêvan mêvanê Xwedê ye.* The guest is God’s guest.

lessons.beat: The second night’s tale: the fox and the bear share a field, fairly, they agree. Each year the bear chooses the top half or the bottom, and each year the fox has planted the crop that leaves the bear only what is bitter or tasteless: the roots of the wheat, the stalks of the maize. The bear sulks so loudly that Hevalo hides behind the stove. Hamo does the bear’s voice, very well.

Dapîr answers each tale with a proverb, and Hamo explains each proverb with another tale, which Dapîr answers with another proverb: drop by drop, water becomes a lake; a sweet tongue brings the snake out of its hole; the guest is God’s guest; however high the mountain… Nobody goes to bed.

new.ku: Zimanê şîrîn mar ji qulê derdixe.
new.en: A sweet tongue brings the snake out of its hole.
Drop by drop, water becomes a lake.

new.ku: Çiya çiqas bilind be, wê rê pê keve.
new.en: However high the mountain, a road will cross it.

lessons.beat: A proverb duel: you and the children against Dapîr, with Hamo as judge, saying each of Dapîr’s answers aloud. Every problem has its proverb and its solution, and Dapîr, the wisest person in the valley, always has the last word. Then Hevalo walks in with an apple in his mouth, and Hamo, the joker, says that Hevalo’s answer to every problem is an apple.

In the middle of the laughter Hamo’s phone rings: a call from Kobanî, the town where he grew up. Hamo tells the caller about the proverb duel, everyone shouts a proverb down the line, and Dapîr, as always, has the last word.

skills.grammar: everything together: present, past, future and wishes in one farewell (… pîroz be, … vekirî be, … sax be)
skills.grammarMd:
**Rêya te vekirî be!** May your road be open! A wish ends in *be*, and you can make one from anything you know: *Destê te sax be!* · *Cejna te pîroz be!* · *Rêya te vekirî be!*

- One goodbye can hold the whole road: *Tu hatî, tu kurdî fêr bûyî, tu yê vegerî, û tu yê dîsa bêyî!* You came, you learnt Kurdish, you will go back, and you will come again!

lessons.beat: Spring again, and the square is full for Ferhad’s son’s wedding: the bride on a white horse, the groom’s family singing, the big drum and the zurna, the women’s joyful cries. It is also the village’s farewell for its teacher, who leaves for Hewlêr at the end of the week. The govend winds round the square, Hamo at its head, waving his handkerchief, and even Bozo, it is said, dances.

Xezo’s goodbye speech to everyone, and Hamo passes her words on to those at the back: thank you for everything, for every tale, for every glass of tea. “Ez ê bêriya we hemûyan bikim.” Then she turns to Hamo and cannot finish.

new.en: Goodbye, everyone! (said by the one leaving)

lessons.beat: Dawn at the blue gate, where your road began, and the bus is waiting. Hamo, Hevalo and you say goodbye to Xezo. “Rêya te vekirî be, Xezo!” says Hamo; “Xwedê ji te razî be!” “Oxir be, bi silametî!” Then, outraged and proud, he tells you her parting order: he is to take care of his moustache. Hevalo gets the last apple.

new.en: Safe journey! (may your road be open)
Farewell! Good luck! (to someone setting off)
gate (a yard’s big door: Hamo’s blue gate is a dergeh)

lessons.beat: The bus has gone round the bend, and the village turns to you: your road is ending too. At the blue gate everyone blesses you on your way (Nazê and the children, Dapîr, Mîrza and Bişar, and Hevalo with an apple) and Hamo shows you the sapling he planted for you under the old apple tree. You came, you learnt Kurdish, and you understand every word he says: “Rêya te vekirî be!” The end of the road, and the beginning of yours.

doubts.reason: the answer to “Bi xêr hatî!”: the owner chose “Xêra Xwedê li we bê!” over “Ser çavan!”

taught in chapter 1 as “What is it in Kurdish?”; “Bi kurdî jê re çi dibêjin?” is the fuller way — confirm the short one sounds natural
taught whole in chapter 1, with dixwazî and dixwaze, before the present tense (chapter 4) — confirm the forms

well done: spelt aferîn; some write aferin — confirm

zozan: dictionaries disagree on its gender; the course takes it as feminine and mostly uses it in the plural (li zozanan) — confirm
